title: ReactWidgets — Building Mini Apps with React
subtitle: A step-by-step recap of recent work to prepare for the next phase.

sections.text: Overview
ReactWidgets is a collection of interactive mini-apps built with React 19, Vite 8, and Tailwind CSS 4. This post documents the recent setup, component builds, styling improvements, and next steps.
Step 1: Project Scaffolding
Initialized the project with Vite and React, then installed dependencies including Tailwind CSS v4 with the Vite plugin, Sass, and React Router.

npm create vite@latest reactwidgets -- --template react
npm install react-router-dom sass-embedded @tailwindcss/vite
Step 2: Weather Widget

Built a weather widget that fetches real-time data from the OpenWeatherMap API. Features include city search, dynamic weather icons, and humidity/wind speed display. Styled with a purple gradient background in SCSS.

items: API integration with fetch and environment variable for API key
Dynamic icon mapping based on weather condition codes
Responsive layout for mobile screens

sections.text: Step 3: Calculator Widget

A fully functional calculator supporting basic arithmetic operations. Styled with a dark theme and grid-based button layout in SCSS. The display background was matched to button colors for visual consistency.

items: Grid layout for numeric and operator buttons
Clear, delete, and percentage operations
Dark theme with hover states

sections.text: Step 4: Pomodoro Timer Widget
A productivity timer that cycles between 25-minute focus sessions and 5-minute breaks. Tracks completed sessions in localStorage for persistence across page reloads.

items: 25/5 minute work-break cycle
localStorage persistence for session count
Separated CSS from inline styles
Smooth dark gradient theme

sections.text: Step 5: Navigation & Routing
Set up React Router with pages for Home, Widgets, Portfolio, About, Blog, and Contact. A responsive navigation bar with a hamburger menu toggle on mobile was added.

items: BrowserRouter wrapping the app in main.jsx
Route-based rendering in App.jsx
Sticky nav with gradient branding and animated underline
Mobile hamburger menu with smooth toggle animation

sections.text: Step 6: UI/UX & Responsive Polish
The entire layout was modernized with a dark gradient background, consistent typography, and responsive breakpoints. The Home page now features a hero section with feature cards.

items: Dark gradient global background
Home hero with animated CTA button
Widgets grid using responsive columns
Removed global body styles from Calculator.scss that broke page layout
Fade-in animations on page load

sections.text: Next Preparation
The following areas are ready for the next phase of development:

items: Content pages ready for real content
Blog engine primed for markdown rendering or CMS integration
Calculator refactor needed — replace eval() with a proper expression parser
Additional widgets can be added to the grid
Consider introducing Zustand or Context API for shared state

title: Getting Started with React 19
subtitle: A beginner-friendly guide to building your first React app.

sections.text: Why React?

React is one of the most popular front-end libraries for building user interfaces. With the release of React 19, the developer experience has improved significantly with new features like React Server Components, Actions, and improved hooks.
Setting Up Your First Project
The easiest way to start is with Vite, a fast build tool that provides instant hot module replacement and optimized builds.

npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
Understanding Components
Components are the building blocks of React. A component is a JavaScript function that returns UI elements. You can compose components together to build complex interfaces.

items: Functional components with hooks
Props for passing data between components
State management with useState and useReducer

title: Styling with Tailwind CSS v4
subtitle: Explore the new utility-first workflow in Tailwind CSS v4.

sections.text: What's New in v4
Tailwind CSS v4 introduces a completely redesigned engine built on Lightning CSS, offering faster builds, CSS-first configuration, and a new utility approach.
CSS-First Configuration
Instead of a tailwind.config.js file, v4 uses native CSS with @theme, @utility, and @variant directives. This makes configuration more intuitive and eliminates the config file overhead.
Vite Plugin Integration
The @tailwindcss/vite plugin provides seamless integration with Vite, enabling on-the-fly CSS processing and instant HMR updates.

items: Zero-config setup with Vite plugin
Native CSS @import for Tailwind directives
Faster build times with Lightning CSS

title: Responsive Design Patterns in 2026
subtitle: Modern approaches to building layouts that work everywhere.

sections.text: Mobile-First Mindset

Designing for mobile first forces you to prioritize content and core functionality. You then progressively enhance the experience for larger screens using CSS Grid, media queries, and container queries.
CSS Grid for Layouts
CSS Grid with auto-fit and minmax is the most powerful tool for responsive layouts without media queries. It automatically adjusts columns based on available space.
Container Queries
Container queries allow components to respond to their parent container's size rather than the viewport. This is ideal for reusable components that appear in various contexts.

items: Use @container for component-level responsiveness
Combine with CSS Grid for flexible layouts
Avoid excessive media queries for reusable components

title: Building a Contact Form with React — Step by Step
subtitle: A hands-on guide to creating a fully functional contact form with localStorage persistence and an embedded map.

sections.text: Overview

In this post, we walk through building a contact form component in React. The form collects name, email, phone number, subject, and a message — then saves submissions to localStorage and shows a success state. We also add a location map using an OpenStreetMap iframe.
Step 1: Setting Up State
We use a single form state object to track all input fields. Each field's value is updated via a shared handleChange handler that uses the input's name attribute.
Step 2: Form Layout
The form uses a two-column grid for name/email and phone/subject pairs, with the message textarea spanning the full width. Each field is wrapped in a form-group div with a label and styled input.
Step 3: Form Submission & localStorage
On submit, we prevent the default browser behavior, read existing messages from localStorage, append the new entry with a timestamp, and save it back. Then we show a success view.
Step 4: Success State
When submitted is true, we render a success message with a green checkmark icon and a 'Send Another' button that resets the submitted state back to the form.
Step 5: Adding a Location Map

Beside the form, we embed an OpenStreetMap iframe. This provides a visual location reference without needing a Google Maps API key. The map is wrapped in a container with rounded corners and an address label below.
Our Location
Step 6: Responsive Layout
The form and map sit side by side on desktop using flexbox. On screens narrower than 800px, they stack vertically. The form rows also collapse from two columns to one at 600px.
Key Takeaways

items: Use a single state object with a generic handleChange for simple forms
localStorage is perfect for client-side demo persistence — no backend needed
A success state provides clear feedback after form submission
OpenStreetMap iframes are a free, API-key-free alternative for embedded maps
Flexbox with media queries keeps the layout clean across screen sizes
